questions.q: In the phase I flowchart, a prodrug that is inactive is converted to an:
opts: Activated form after the drug is broken down
questions.exp: The phase I flow shows prodrug (inactive) - drug broken down - activated; the other limb shows most drugs (active) - inactivated. (Book p11)

questions.q: For MOST drugs, which are already active, phase I metabolism results in:
opts: Inactivation of the drug, adding a functional group
Activation of the drug, removing a functional group
Direct conjugation without any functional group
questions.exp: Most drugs are active; phase I breaks them down into the inactivated form with a functional group, which is then handled by phase II. (Book p11)

questions.q: The product of phase I metabolism that enters phase II is:
questions.exp: Phase I yields drug + functional group, which is the substrate for phase II conjugation. (Book p11)

questions.q: In phase II, the drug with its functional group is combined with a conjugate which is:
questions.exp: The flowchart labels the conjugate as -ve charged, which makes the drug ionized and water soluble. (Book p11)

questions.q: The end product of phase II metabolism is:
opts: Ionized and water soluble, hence easily excreted
questions.exp: Drug + functional group + conjugate becomes ionized and water soluble and is easily excreted - the object of phase II. (Book p11)

questions.q: The purpose of conjugation in phase II metabolism is to:
opts: Make the drug water soluble and easily excretable
Make the drug more lipid soluble for absorption
Activate the drug at its receptor
questions.exp: Conjugation with a negatively charged group makes the metabolite ionized and water soluble, so it is easily excreted. (Book p11)

questions.q: According to the note on this page, a placebo:
opts: Contains a conjugate of the active drug
Contains the drug in subtherapeutic dose
questions.exp: The note plainly states that placebo does not contain any drug - it is used for its psychological effect. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes drug metabolism?
opts: Active drug - phase I inactivates it and adds a functional group - phase II conjugates it - water-soluble metabolite excreted
Active drug - phase II conjugates it - phase I inactivates it - lipid-soluble metabolite reabsorbed
Prodrug - phase II conjugation - activation - excretion
Active drug - conjugation - renal tubular reabsorption - excretion
questions.exp: Phase I (CYP450) breaks the drug down and adds a functional group; phase II attaches a charged conjugate to give an ionized water-soluble product that is easily excreted. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of the following is a prodrug among the antimalarials?
questions.exp: Proguanil heads the list of prodrugs - it requires metabolic activation to exert its antimalarial action. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors are NOT prodrugs?
questions.exp: Ramipril and other ACE inhibitors are prodrugs EXCEPT captopril and lisinopril, which are active as such. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of the following pairs are all prodrugs?
questions.exp: Oxcarbazepine and omeprazole appear in the prodrug list, along with proguanil, ramipril, dipivefrine, levodopa, racecadotril, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. (Book p11)

questions.q: Dipivefrine, used in ophthalmology, is listed as a:
questions.exp: Dipivefrine appears in the list of prodrugs given on the page. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of the following anticancer drugs are listed as prodrugs?
questions.exp: 5-Fluorouracil and gemcitabine are included in the prodrug list. (Book p11)

questions.q: Levodopa is grouped with the prodrugs because it:
opts: Must be converted to the active moiety in the body
Is a prodrug that never becomes active
questions.exp: Levodopa is listed among prodrugs - it is inactive as such and is decarboxylated to the active dopamine. (Book p11)

questions.q: Racecadotril and dipivefrine share which property in this list?
questions.exp: Racecadotril and dipivefrine both appear in the prodrug list along with proguanil, ramipril, oxcarbazepine, omeprazole, levodopa, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine. (Book p11)

questions.q: The mnemonic ORCHAD stands for:
questions.exp: ORCHAD lists phase I reactions: Oxidation, Reduction, Cyclization, Hydrolysis, Aliphatic hydroxylation, Aromatic hydroxylation and Deamination. (Book p11)

questions.q: The commonest phase I reaction is:
questions.exp: Oxidation is marked m/c in the ORCHAD list of phase I reactions. (Book p11)

questions.q: Phase I reactions are enabled by:
questions.exp: The page states that phase I reactions are enabled by microsomal CYP450 enzymes - the mixed function oxidases. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a phase I reaction in the ORCHAD list?
questions.exp: Glucuronidation is a phase II conjugation, not a phase I reaction; phase I comprises oxidation, reduction, cyclization, hydrolysis, aliphatic and aromatic hydroxylation and deamination. (Book p11)

questions.q: Phase II reactions are named after:
questions.exp: The page notes phase II reactions are named after the conjugate, e.g. glucuronidation, glycination, glutathionation. (Book p11)

questions.q: The commonest phase II reaction is:
questions.exp: Glucuronidation is marked m/c among phase II reactions, and it is microsomal. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which phase II reaction is a MICROSOMAL reaction?
questions.exp: Glucuronidation (m/c) is grouped as microsomal; glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation are listed as non-microsomal. (Book p11)

questions.q: Which set of phase II reactions is NON-microsomal?
questions.exp: The brace marks glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation as non-microsomal reactions, leaving glucuronidation as the microsomal one. (Book p11)

questions.q: In 'CYP', the CY stands for cytochrome, which is described as a:
opts: Heme protein that binds oxygen and facilitates metabolism
questions.exp: CY (cytochrome) is a heme protein that binds oxygen and thereby facilitates metabolism. (Book p12)

questions.q: The 'P450' designation was given because these enzymes:
opts: Were discovered in plant pigment and absorb light of 450 nm wavelength
Require a pH of 4.50 to work
questions.exp: P450: enzymes discovered in plant pigment, absorbing light of 450 nm wavelength. (Book p12)

questions.q: In the nomenclature CYP1A2, the number 1 denotes the:
questions.exp: In CYP1A2: 1 = family, A = subfamily, 2 = gene/isoform number. (Book p12)

questions.q: In the nomenclature CYP1A2, the letter A denotes the:
questions.exp: The letter A stands for subfamily, while the numeral after it is the gene/isoform number. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which drugs are metabolised by CYP1A2?
questions.exp: CYP1A2 metabolises paracetamol, tacrine and theophylline. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which drugs are metabolised by CYP2B6?
questions.exp: CYP2B6 metabolises 6-mercaptopurine and methyldopa. (Book p12)

questions.q: Phenytoin and warfarin are metabolised by:
questions.exp: CYP2C9 is listed with phenytoin and warfarin as its substrates. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole and:
questions.exp: CYP2C19 metabolises omeprazole and activates clopidogrel, converting the prodrug to its active form. (Book p12)

questions.q: Omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel because:
opts: Both are substrates of CYP2C19, so omeprazole acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme
Omeprazole induces CYP2C19 and destroys clopidogrel
Omeprazole increases gastric pH and prevents clopidogrel absorption
Omeprazole binds clopidogrel directly in plasma
questions.exp: The book marks them as competitive inhibitors (substrates, decreased enzyme): omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel. (Book p12)

questions.q: Clopidogrel requires activation by CYP2C19. A patient with an acute coronary syndrome started on both omeprazole and clopidogrel will have:
opts: A reduced antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel
Enhanced antiplatelet effect with bleeding risk
No interaction because they act on different enzymes
questions.exp: Since omeprazole and clopidogrel compete for the same enzyme, omeprazole decreases the effect of clopidogrel - a loss of antiplatelet protection. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP2D6 metabolises all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: CYP2D6 metabolises psychiatric drugs (antidepressants and antipsychotics), opioids and beta blockers; mifepristone is the example given for CYP3A4. (Book p12)

questions.q: CYP2D6 ACTIVATES which of the following?
questions.exp: CYP2D6 activates tamoxifen, converting the prodrug to its active metabolite. (Book p12)

questions.q: A patient on tamoxifen started on a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor is at risk of:
opts: Reduced activation of tamoxifen and loss of efficacy
No interaction, since tamoxifen is excreted unchanged
Increased activation of tamoxifen with toxicity
questions.exp: Tamoxifen is activated by CYP2D6; inhibiting the enzyme reduces formation of the active metabolite and lowers efficacy. (Book p12)

questions.q: Chronic consumption of ethanol causes:
questions.exp: The flowchart runs ethanol - chronic consumption - CYP2E1 upregulation. (Book p12)

questions.q: In a chronic alcoholic, paracetamol produces hepatotoxicity because CYP2E1 upregulation leads to:
questions.exp: The flow reads: paracetamol - increased NAPQI - hepatotoxicity, following CYP2E1 upregulation by chronic alcohol. (Book p12)

questions.q: Paracetamol is metabolised predominantly by:
questions.exp: The book notes paracetamol is metabolised by CYP2E1 >> CYP1A2 - which is why alcohol-induced CYP2E1 upregulation is so dangerous. (Book p12)

questions.q: NAPQI is best described as:
opts: The toxic metabolite of paracetamol whose rise causes hepatotoxicity
The active analgesic metabolite of paracetamol
A glutathione conjugate excreted in bile
An enzyme inducer present in alcohol
questions.exp: The flowchart links paracetamol to increased NAPQI and thence hepatotoxicity - NAPQI is the hepatotoxic metabolite. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which CYP enzyme is the commonest (m/c) and metabolises more than 50% of drugs?
questions.exp: CYP3A4 is marked m/c and metabolises >50% of drugs, with mifepristone given as an example. (Book p12)

questions.q: Mifepristone is given as the example of a drug metabolised by:
questions.exp: The example quoted for CYP3A4, which metabolises more than half of all drugs, is mifepristone. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which CYP drug-substrate pair is correctly matched?
questions.exp: CYP2C9 handles phenytoin and warfarin; methyldopa is a CYP2B6 substrate, theophylline a CYP1A2 substrate and mifepristone a CYP3A4 example. (Book p12)

questions.q: Which antiviral drug causes Steven Johnson syndrome through glucuronidation issues?
questions.exp: The glucuronidation section lists atazanavir (antiviral) causing Steven Johnson syndrome. (Book p13)

questions.q: Irinotecan, an anticancer drug, is associated with toxicity because of:
questions.exp: The page pairs irinotecan (anticancer) with toxicity under the heading glucuronidation. (Book p13)

questions.q: Atazanavir and irinotecan are contraindicated in:
questions.exp: Both atazanavir and irinotecan are contraindicated in Crigler Najjar syndrome, where glucuronidation is defective. (Book p13)

questions.q: Atazanavir and irinotecan share which single contraindication in the book?
questions.exp: The brace on the page ties atazanavir-induced Steven Johnson syndrome and irinotecan toxicity to one contraindication - Crigler Najjar syndrome. (Book p13)

questions.q: Estrogen is metabolised in the liver by:
opts: Phase I with CYP3A4 followed by phase II glucuronidation
Phase I with CYP2E1 followed by acetylation
Phase II acetylation followed by hydrolysis
questions.exp: The estrogen flowchart shows liver phase I with CYP3A4 and phase II glucuronidation. (Book p13)

questions.q: In the liver, estrogen is converted to estrogen + glucuronic acid, which is:
questions.exp: Estrogen + glucuronic acid is labelled water soluble, allowing it to be carried to the small intestine. (Book p13)

questions.q: Enterohepatic circulation of estrogen begins when gut bacteria act on estrogen glucuronide by:
questions.exp: In the small intestine, glucuronidase action by gut bacteria breaks down the conjugate; estrogen is then broken down to a lipid-soluble form that is reabsorbed. (Book p13)

questions.q: Enterohepatic circulation of a drug results in:
questions.exp: The boxed point states enterohepatic circulation is an extension of the normal T1/2, because drug is reabsorbed repeatedly instead of being excreted. (Book p13)

questions.q: Antibiotics cause oral contraceptive pill failure by:
opts: Decreasing the enterohepatic circulation of estrogen, so its T1/2 falls
Increasing the enterohepatic circulation of estrogen
Blocking estrogen receptors in the uterus
questions.exp: Antibiotics kill gut bacteria, so less glucuronidase deconjugates estrogen; enterohepatic circulation falls, T1/2 falls and OCP failure results. (Book p13)

questions.q: The sequence leading to oral contraceptive failure with antibiotics is:
opts: Antibiotics - decreased enterohepatic circulation of estrogen - decreased T1/2 - OCP failure
Antibiotics - increased enterohepatic circulation - increased T1/2 - OCP failure
Antibiotics - increased CYP3A4 - decreased estrogen - OCP failure
Antibiotics - decreased gut glucuronidase - increased estrogen - OCP failure
questions.exp: The flowchart reads antibiotics - down enterohepatic circulation of estrogen - down T1/2 - OCP failure. (Book p13)

questions.q: For estrogen to re-enter the enterohepatic circulation after bacterial deconjugation, it must become:
questions.exp: After glucuronidase action the estrogen is 'broken down + lipid soluble', which allows reabsorption and re-entry into the circulation. (Book p13)

questions.q: The mnemonic HIPS Dance stands for drugs undergoing:
opts: Acetylation, and capable of causing drug-induced SLE
Glucuronidation, and capable of causing Steven Johnson syndrome
Sulfation, and capable of causing cholestasis
Oxidation, and capable of causing hepatotoxicity
questions.exp: HIPS Dance lists acetylated drugs - Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide, Dapsone - which can cause drug-induced SLE. (Book p13)

questions.q: Which group of drugs can cause drug-induced SLE?
questions.exp: The brace groups all five HIPS Dance drugs as capable of causing drug-induced SLE. (Book p13)

questions.q: In the HIPS Dance mnemonic, the letters stand for:
questions.exp: HIPS Dance: Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide and Dapsone - all acetylated, all capable of drug-induced SLE. (Book p13)

questions.q: A patient on isoniazid for tuberculosis develops fever, arthralgia and a positive ANA. The likely cause is:
opts: Drug-induced SLE from an acetylated drug
questions.exp: Isoniazid belongs to the HIPS Dance group of acetylated drugs that can cause drug-induced SLE. (Book p13)

questions.q: Microsomal enzyme inducers increase metabolism and thereby cause plasma concentration to fall, resulting in:
questions.exp: The inducer column reads: increased enzyme - increased metabolism - plasma concentration falls - drug failure. (Book p14)

questions.q: Microsomal enzyme inhibitors decrease metabolism, so plasma concentration rises and produces:
questions.exp: The inhibitor column reads: decreased enzyme - decreased metabolism - increased plasma concentration - drug toxicity. (Book p14)

questions.q: Enzyme induction causes drug failure because:
opts: More enzyme means faster metabolism and a lower plasma concentration
More enzyme means slower metabolism and a higher plasma concentration
Enzyme induction blocks the drug at its receptor
questions.exp: Induction increases the amount of enzyme, speeds metabolism, lowers plasma concentration and thereby causes failure of therapy. (Book p14)

questions.q: Enzyme inhibition causes drug toxicity because:
opts: Less enzyme means slower metabolism and a higher plasma concentration
Less enzyme means faster metabolism and a lower plasma concentration
Inhibitors increase the number of receptors
questions.exp: Enzyme inhibition reduces metabolism, so the drug accumulates, plasma concentration rises and toxicity follows. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which of the following are enzyme inducers?
opts: Griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, phenobarbital, carbamazepine
Grapefruit juice, acute alcohol, diethylcarbamazine, neratinib
questions.exp: The inducer list is griseofulvin, rifampicin, alcohol (chronic), benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort. (Book p14)

questions.q: St. John's wort, listed as an enzyme inducer, is a plant used to treat:
questions.exp: The book annotates St. John's wort as 'plant used to treat depression', and lists it among enzyme inducers. (Book p14)

questions.q: Benzopyrene, listed among enzyme inducers, is encountered in:
questions.exp: Benzopyrene appears in the inducer list - it is a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon of cigarette smoke that induces CYP1A2. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an enzyme inducer as listed in the table?
questions.exp: Ketoconazole is an enzyme INHIBITOR; inducers are griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, benzopyrene, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which of the following are enzyme inhibitors?
questions.exp: The inhibitor list is acute alcohol consumption, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice and diethylcarbamazine. (Book p14)

questions.q: Regarding alcohol, the table specifies that:
opts: Acute alcohol consumption is an inhibitor while chronic alcohol is an inducer
Both acute and chronic alcohol are inducers
Both acute and chronic alcohol are inhibitors
Alcohol does not affect microsomal enzymes
questions.exp: Chronic alcohol appears in the inducer column and acute alcohol consumption in the inhibitor column - the same agent with opposite effects by duration of intake. (Book p14)

questions.q: Grapefruit juice is listed as an:
questions.exp: Grapefruit juice appears in the inhibitor column, with cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate and others. (Book p14)

questions.q: Diethylcarbamazine is listed as an enzyme:
questions.exp: Diethylcarbamazine appears at the end of the enzyme inhibitor list. (Book p14)

questions.q: Isoniazid appears in the table as an enzyme:
questions.exp: Isoniazid is listed among enzyme inhibitors, along with quinidine, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole and valproate. (Book p14)

questions.q: In oral contraceptive failure due to rifampicin, the book's options include all EXCEPT:
opts: Changing the method of contraception (IUD or condoms)
Increasing the dose of drugs such as phenytoin and retigabine
questions.exp: The three options given are to change the method of contraception (IUD or condoms), avoid enzyme inducers, or increase the dose of drugs like phenytoin and retigabine. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which two drugs are named as examples whose dose may be increased when an enzyme inducer is unavoidable?
questions.exp: The page gives phenytoin and retigabine as examples of drugs whose dose can be increased in the face of enzyme induction. (Book p14)

questions.q: A woman on rifampicin for tuberculosis on combined oral contraceptives experiences OCP failure because rifampicin:
opts: Induces microsomal enzymes, accelerating estrogen metabolism
Inhibits microsomal enzymes, delaying estrogen metabolism
Kills gut bacteria and reduces enterohepatic circulation
Competes with estrogen at the receptor
questions.exp: Rifampicin is a classic enzyme inducer: it increases metabolism of the contraceptive steroids, reduces their plasma concentration and causes OCP failure. (Book p14)

questions.q: Erythromycin inhibits microsomal enzymes and therefore causes:
opts: Theophylline toxicity, with ventricular arrhythmia and ventricular fibrillation
questions.exp: The clinical significance box states erythromycin leads to theophylline toxicity presenting as ventricular arrhythmia and ventricular fibrillation. (Book p14)

questions.q: Clarithromycin, by enzyme inhibition, causes:
questions.exp: The page pairs clarithromycin with statin toxicity - inhibition of statin metabolism raises levels and causes myopathy. (Book p14)

questions.q: A patient on a statin develops muscle pain after being prescribed clarithromycin. The mechanism is:
opts: Enzyme inhibition raising statin plasma concentration
Reduced statin absorption from the gut
questions.exp: Clarithromycin inhibits microsomal enzymes, so the statin accumulates and toxicity (myopathy) follows - the stated clarithromycin-statin toxicity. (Book p14)

questions.q: A patient with asthma on theophylline presents with ventricular arrhythmia after starting erythromycin. The best explanation is:
opts: Erythromycin inhibits theophylline metabolism, causing theophylline toxicity
Erythromycin induces theophylline metabolism, causing theophylline failure
questions.exp: Erythromycin is an enzyme inhibitor; theophylline levels rise and toxicity manifests as ventricular arrhythmia and ventricular fibrillation. (Book p14)

questions.q: Rifampicin and cimetidine differ in that rifampicin is an ______ while cimetidine is an ______.
questions.exp: Rifampicin appears in the inducer column and cimetidine in the inhibitor column of the drug interaction table. (Book p14)

questions.q: Which statement about chronic versus acute alcohol is correct?
opts: Chronic consumption induces enzymes causing drug failure, acute consumption inhibits enzymes causing drug toxicity
Chronic consumption inhibits enzymes while acute consumption induces them
Both chronic and acute consumption cause identical effects
Only acute consumption affects microsomal enzymes
questions.exp: Chronic alcohol is listed as an inducer (drug failure) and acute alcohol consumption as an inhibitor (drug toxicity). (Book p14)

units.title: Phase I and Phase II: The Two Steps
units.guide: Phase I either activates an inactive prodrug or inactivates a drug, and always leaves it with a functional group. Phase II then attaches a negatively charged conjugate to give a drug + functional group + conjugate that is ionized and water soluble and therefore easily excreted. A placebo, by definition, contains no drug at all.

units.title: Prodrugs and Their Examples
units.guide: Prodrugs are inactive as given and need metabolic activation: proguanil, ramipril and other ACE inhibitors except captopril and lisinopril, oxcarbazepine, omeprazole, dipivefrine, levodopa, racecadotril, 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine.

units.title: ORCHAD and the Phase II Conjugations
units.sec: Reactions of Drugs in the Phases · p11
units.guide: Phase I reactions follow ORCHAD - oxidation (commonest), reduction, cyclization, hydrolysis, aliphatic hydroxylation, aromatic hydroxylation and deamination - and are enabled by microsomal CYP450 enzymes. Phase II reactions are named after the conjugate: glucuronidation is the commonest and is microsomal, while glycination, glutathionation, acetylation, methylation and sulfation are non-microsomal.

units.title: CYP450: What the Name Means
units.guide: CY is a cytochrome - a heme protein that binds oxygen and so facilitates metabolism - and the P450 tag comes from enzymes discovered in plant pigment that absorb light at 450 nm. In CYP1A2 the numerals and letter read as family 1, subfamily A and gene/isoform number 2.

units.title: Isoform by Isoform: 1A2, 2B6 and 2C9
units.sec: Drugs metabolised in phase I · p12
units.guide: CYP1A2 metabolises paracetamol, tacrine and theophylline; CYP2B6 metabolises 6-mercaptopurine and methyldopa; CYP2C9 metabolises phenytoin and warfarin.

units.title: CYP2C19: Omeprazole vs Clopidogrel
units.guide: CYP2C19 both metabolises omeprazole and activates the prodrug clopidogrel. Because both are substrates competing for a limited amount of enzyme, omeprazole behaves as a competitive inhibitor and decreases the effect of clopidogrel - so the combination loses antiplatelet protection.

units.title: CYP2D6 and Tamoxifen Activation
units.guide: CYP2D6 metabolises psychiatric drugs (antidepressants and antipsychotics), opioids and beta blockers, and it activates tamoxifen. Inhibiting CYP2D6 therefore deprives the patient of tamoxifen's active metabolite and reduces its efficacy.

units.title: CYP2E1, Alcohol and Paracetamol
units.guide: Chronic alcohol consumption upregulates CYP2E1, and paracetamol is metabolised by CYP2E1 far more than by CYP1A2. The induced enzyme diverts paracetamol into its toxic metabolite NAPQI, so a chronic alcoholic taking paracetamol develops hepatotoxicity at doses that would otherwise be safe.

units.title: CYP3A4: The Commonest Isoform
units.guide: CYP3A4 is the commonest CYP enzyme, metabolising more than 50% of all drugs - mifepristone is the example given. Putting the isoforms side by side, methyldopa belongs to CYP2B6, theophylline to CYP1A2, mifepristone to CYP3A4 and warfarin to CYP2C9.

units.title: Glucuronidation Failure: Crigler Najjar
units.guide: Glucuronidation is the phase II reaction of concern in two drugs: atazanavir, an antiviral that causes Steven Johnson syndrome, and irinotecan, an anticancer drug that causes toxicity. Both are contraindicated in Crigler Najjar syndrome, in which glucuronidation is defective and the drugs cannot be cleared safely.

units.title: Enterohepatic Circulation of Estrogen
units.guide: Estrogen is handled in the liver by phase I CYP3A4 then phase II glucuronidation, yielding the water-soluble estrogen-glucuronic acid. Gut bacterial glucuronidase liberates lipid-soluble estrogen that is reabsorbed - enterohepatic circulation, which extends the normal half-life. Antibiotics kill those bacteria, so enterohepatic circulation and T1/2 fall and the oral contraceptive fails.

units.title: HIPS Dance: Acetylation and Drug-Induced SLE
units.guide: Acetylation is a non-microsomal phase II reaction, and the drugs that undergo it are recalled by HIPS Dance: Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Sulfonamide and Dapsone. All five can produce drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus - so arthralgia, fever and a positive ANA in a patient on isoniazid should raise that possibility.

units.title: Induction vs Inhibition: The Core Effect
units.guide: Microsomal enzyme induction raises enzyme amount and metabolism, lowers plasma concentration and causes drug failure; enzyme inhibition does the reverse - less metabolism, higher plasma concentration and drug toxicity. Every interaction in this table is read off that single axis.

units.title: The Inducer List
units.guide: Enzyme inducers are griseofulvin, rifampicin, chronic alcohol, benzopyrene (cigarette smoke), phenobarbital, carbamazepine and St. John's wort - the plant used to treat depression. Recognizing them matters because they silently produce therapeutic failure of co-prescribed drugs.

units.title: The Inhibitor List and Alcohol's Two Faces
units.guide: Enzyme inhibitors include acute alcohol consumption, quinidine, isoniazid, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, ketoconazole, valproate, erythromycin/clarithromycin, grapefruit juice and diethylcarbamazine. Alcohol is unique in appearing on both sides: acute intake inhibits while chronic intake induces.

units.title: Clinical Payoff: OCP Failure, Theophylline and Statins
units.guide: The clinical payoff of this table is memorised as four vignettes: rifampicin induces enzymes and causes OCP failure - manage by switching to an IUD or condoms, avoiding inducers, or raising the dose of drugs such as phenytoin and retigabine; erythromycin causes theophylline toxicity with ventricular arrhythmia and fibrillation; clarithromycin causes statin toxicity; and alcohol's effect depends on whether intake is acute or chronic.
